description: Core Serbian building blocks for conversation, level A2–B1, standard ekavian Serbian in Latin script.

terms.definition: Says who someone is, what something is like, or where it is. Short forms: sam, si, je, smo, ste, su.
terms.example: Gde si? U autobusu sam. — Where are you? I'm on the bus.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Sam umoran' for 'I'm tired': a short form can't start a sentence. Say 'Umoran sam'.

terms.definition: There is, there isn't: ima kafić blizu, nema hleba.
terms.example: Ima li mleka? Nema, sve smo popili. — Is there milk? No, we drank it all.
terms.anti_example: Not 'nema mleko': after nema the noun changes its ending, so 'nema mleka', 'nema vremena'.

terms.definition: Want something, or want to do it: hoću kafu, hoću da spavam.
terms.example: Hoću da idem kući, umorna sam. — I want to go home, I'm tired.
terms.discussion: Hoću sounds pushy when you order. In a café say 'Jednu kafu, molim' or 'Mogu li dobiti kafu?'

terms.definition: Makes a verb negative. It goes right before the verb and is written apart: ne znam.
terms.example: Izvinite, ne znam gde je pošta. — Sorry, I don't know where the post office is.
terms.anti_example: Not 'ne sam' or 'ne imam': with biti, imati and hteti it joins the verb, so nisam, nemam, neću.

terms.definition: Have or own something. The negative is one word: nemam, nemaš, nema.
terms.example: Imaš li olovku? Moja ne piše. — Got a pen? Mine doesn't work.
terms.anti_example: Not 'imam da idem' for 'I have to go': imati is only 'own'. Say 'moram da idem'.

terms.definition: Turns a normal sentence into a yes/no question when you put it first.
terms.example: Da li radiš sutra? — Are you working tomorrow?
terms.discussion: In speech people often drop it and just raise the voice, or put li after the verb: Radiš li sutra?

terms.definition: Can, be able to. With li it is also the polite way to ask for something: mogu li dobiti vodu?
terms.example: Mogu li da platim karticom? — Can I pay by card?

terms.definition: Go, on foot or in general. Present forms: idem, ideš, ide.
terms.example: Idem u prodavnicu, treba li ti nešto? — I'm going to the shop, need anything?
terms.discussion: Idemo! is the everyday 'Let's go!', often with ajde in front: Ajde, idemo!

terms.definition: Must, have to. Add da and a present verb: moram da radim.
terms.example: Moram da idem, mama me čeka. — I have to go, Mom's waiting.
terms.anti_example: Not 'ne moram' for 'I mustn't': ne moram means you don't have to. For not allowed, say ne smem.

terms.definition: Come or arrive, as one finished event: kad dođeš, when you get here.
terms.example: Kad dođeš kući, pošalji mi poruku. — Text me when you get home.
terms.anti_example: Not 'Dođem sutra' alone for 'I'm coming tomorrow': say 'Doći ću sutra' or 'Dolazim sutra'.

relationships.description: English 'have to' is morati, never imati: moram da idem.
Idem is going away from here; dođi is coming toward the speaker.
Same verb forms, but ima / nema says what exists, while imati says who owns it.
